paper_title: OmniSpectra: A Unified Foundation Model for Universal Spectra Representation Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Standard sequence models encode position by token rank rather than physical coordinate, typically forcing practitioners to destructively resample continuous physical signals such as spectra observed across heterogeneous instruments. We identify this coordinate mismatch as a structural limitation in cross-instrument representation learning, and propose OmniSpectra, a wavelength-native foundation model for spectral representation learning: a continuous-coordinate masked autoencoder that discards the integer pixel indexing of sequence modeling. Mapping physical coordinates to a logarithmic basis turns the multiplicative scaling induced by cosmological redshift into a uniform additive shift. In continuous rotary position embeddings, this shared shift cancels from relative token distances rather than producing grid-dependent positional distortion. We further counter the spectral bias inherent to implicit neural decoders with a physics-grounded, resolution-gated Fourier decoder that provides anti-aliasing. Pretrained on eight surveys and benchmarked against seven baselines, our model reaches state-of-the-art performance with only 12.2M parameters while outperforming substantially larger models, indicating that encoding physical structure can substitute for parameter scale.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Standard sequence models encode position by token rank rather than physical coordinate, typically forcing practitioners to destructively resample continuous physical signals such as spectra observed across heterogeneous instruments. We identify this coordinate mismatch as structural limitation in cross-instrument representation learning, and propose OmniSpectra, wavelength-native foundation model for spectral representation learning: continuous-coordinate masked autoencoder that discards the integer pixel indexing of sequence modeling. Mapping physical coordinates to logarithmic basis turns the multiplicative scaling induced by cosmological redshift into uniform additive shift. In continuous rotary position embeddings, this shared shift cancels from relative token distances rather than producing grid-dependent positional distortion. We further counter the spectral bias inherent to implicit neural decoders with physics-grounded, resolutiongated Fourier decoder that provides anti-aliasing. Pretrained on eight surveys and benchmarked against seven baselines, our model reaches state-of-the-art performance with only 12.2M parameters while outperforming substantially larger models, indicating that encoding physical structure can substitute for parameter scale. Introduction central challenge in representation learning is building one model that generalizes across data sources with heterogeneous structure, resolution, coordinate systems, or sampling density, without dataset-specific preprocessing. Astronomy presents this at scale: spectroscopic surveys already cover hundreds of millions of objects across many instruments and wavelength regimes (Angeloudi et al. 2024), and the coming decade will add petabytes of high-fidelity data. The heterogeneity forces compromise: either per-instrument models, or homogenization by lossy resampling, which blurs narrow high-frequency features such as absorption and emission lines and injects interpolation artifacts into the measurements. Source classification, redshift estimation, and stellar and galaxy property prediction would all benefit from shared representation, but only if it can ingest native spectra from heterogeneous instruments without resampling. Standard sequence models learn structural relationships purely from data, which is sample-inefficient and leaves the Copyright 2027, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved. representation tied to each instruments sampling grid. This alignment challenge has driven wave of multimodal astronomical foundation models: contrastive frameworks (Parker et al. 2024), omnimodal architectures with modality-specific tokenizers (Parker et al. 2025), and generative autoencoders (Melchior et al. 2023). critical obstacle remains: instruments sample the same wavelength range at different pixel densities. When tokenization and positional encoding are defined over the pixel index, feature such as the Hα line falls at different pixel on each detector (Fig. 2a), so one physical wavelength gets different code per survey. The mismatch is structural: even when tokens carry continuous wavelength, attention geometry stays tied to sequence index, so cross-survey weight sharing requires lossy resampling and representations transfer poorly. Our approach. We introduce OmniSpectra  (Fig. 1)  , wavelength-native approach to representation learning that replaces integer pixel indexing with physically anchored logarithmic wavelength coordinates. It factorizes the problem: hardware-efficient fixed-pixel spans extract local line shape from discrete detectors, while shared continuous log λ space unifies the resulting tokens, so attention operates in physical rather than detector space. Coupled with resolution-aware implicit Fourier decoder, one set of weights ingests heterogeneous spectra without fixed grid. OmniSpectras core innovation is evaluating token distance in log λ space  (Table 1)  , reducing positional distance to the physical ratio of wavelengths and grounding parameter-efficient, continuous-coordinate attention geometry in physics. Our contributions are threefold: (i) unified wavelength-anchored positional encoding, realized with continuous 1D Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE), that unifies heterogeneous instruments without interpolation; (ii) Figure 1: OmniSpectra architecture. The encoder extracts local morphology and places tokens in continuous physical logwavelength (log λ) space, where redshift dilation becomes translation. The cross-attention Fourier decoder reconstructs at native coordinates, with an LSF gate tied to the instruments resolution. resolution-gated implicit Fourier decoder that reconstructs at each instruments native coordinates with reduced discretization artifacts or hallucinations; and (iii) unified multi-instrument pretraining framework that handles heterogeneous grids efficiently. Pretrained on 6.4M spectra from eight surveys, OmniSpectra matches or exceeds specialized models on source classification, stellar and galaxy property estimation, and redshift prediction, without resampling or per-instrument adaptation. Related Work Continuous-coordinate models. Perceiver (Jaegle et al. 2022) and NaViT (Dehghani et al. 2023) accept variablelength inputs but still identify observations by index-based positional codes, so one physical feature gets different codes across sampling densities. Relative-position methods such as RoPE (Su et al. 2024) and ALiBi (Press, Smith, and Lewis 2022) improve length generalization by conditioning attention on distances between token indices, but token rank stays instrument-dependent, leaving cross-instrument misalignment unresolved. Neural operators (Li et al. 2021), implicit neural representations (Sitzmann et al. 2020), and set-based models (Lee et al. 2019; Zaheer et al. 2017) instead act directly on continuous coordinates and accommodate irregular sampling. The same mismatch recurs across the sciences: instrument-agnostic Earth-observation models condition on each bands physical wavelength (Xiong et al. 2025), neural implicit methods ingest raw measurement coordinates in MRI (Huang et al. 2023), and mass-spectrometry models embed each peaks continuous m/z (Bushuiev et al. 2026), while fixed-grid laboratory spectroscopy transfers poorly (Koddenbrock et al. 2026). Physics-informed representations. Domain structure in learned representations can improve sample efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization (Wang et al. 2023; Thomas et al. 2018); for spectra it must capture both the location and the fine-scale structure of the signal. Fourier feature networks (Tancik et al. 2020) address spectral bias (Rahaman et al. 2019): standard MLPs fit low frequencies first, property of the networks own Fourier spectrum, not the observed spectrum. This lets coordinate-conditioned decoders recover narrow, high-frequency features. OmniSpectra uses this principle to reconstruct flux continuously at each instruments native wavelength coordinates. Spectroscopic models. Most spectroscopic foundation models remain tied to one instrument and its fixed pixel grid. AstroCLIP (Parker et al. 2024) encodes fixed-length spectra on the native detector grid, but its positional encoding carries no wavelength information; GalSpecNet (Wu et al. 2024) and SpecPT (Pattnaik, Kartaltepe, and Binu 2025) likewise perform strongly within individual surveys without addressing cross-instrument sampling. Spender (Melchior et al. 2023) incorporates physical structure analytically, using the known redshift to resample observations onto common restframe grid; this avoids learning the transformation, but requires at training and inference and stays tied to fixed grid. Recent work addresses broader heterogeneity: AION1 (Parker et al. 2025) tokenizes each instrument separately, and Shen et al. (2025) pretrain one encoderdecoder on native grids with an absolute sinusoidal embedding of λ. OmniSpectra instead makes the coordinate relative and logarithmic, so redshift is uniform translation in attention.

Cosmological redshift maps every rest-frame wavelength according to λobs = (1 + z) λrest, applying the same factor across the spectrum. Index position instead measures separation in token steps, so this mapping changes the number of intervening tokens and hence their positional distance by an amount set by the instruments sampling grid (Fig. 3ab). Redshift is additive in log-wavelength. In log λ the same mapping is additive, log λobs = log λrest + log(1 + z) (5) so one redshift displaces every line by the same offset, the property that motivates uniform log λ binning in spectroscopic pipelines (Bolton et al. 2012) (Fig. 3c). We pretrain on 6.4M spectra from eight surveys: SDSS Legacy, BOSS, eBOSS, SEGUE-1, SEGUE-2, and DESI (optical), plus APOGEE and GALAH (near-infrared, high-resolution) (York et al. 2000; Eisenstein et al. 2011; Blanton et al. 2017; Abdurrouf et al. 2022; Buder et al. 2021; Adame et al. 2024). These span resolving power 1,50034,000 (higher resolves finer detail) and 3,865 16,384 native pixels per spectrum. Every spectrum enters at its native grid, with no resampling or interpolation; persurvey statistics are in Table A1. Training and Baselines. OmniSpectra has 384-dim, 6layer encoder and 128-dim, 4-layer decoder (12.2M parameters). Each valid =32-pixel patch is masked independently with probability 0.5. It is pretrained for 200 epochs on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs with AdamW (lr 104, weight decay 0.05, cosine annealing, batch size 64). We compare four pretrained modelsAstroCLIP, AION-1, Shen et al., and Perceivertwo supervised single-instrument models, GalSpecNet and Spender, and GaSNet-III, template-fitting estimator with no transferable representation, on redshift only. Full hyperparameters and baseline configurations are in Technical Appendices and D. Transfer learning protocol. Foundation models are evaluated with frozen encoder and lightweight cross-attention pooling head that maps the token sequence to fixed vector (following AION-1); supervised baselines (GalSpecNet, Spender) are trained end-to-end per task. We train 10 epochs with AdamW (lr=104, weight decay 0.05), batch size 64, selecting the best model by validation loss. Downstream data splits. Galaxy property and redshift estimation use DESI EDR (Adame et al. 2024) cross-matched with DESI PROVABGS (Hahn et al. 2023) (232.7K samples, 80:20 split); all other tasks use 12,500 random samples per instrument, 20% held out. Results average over 5 random seeds. Evaluation metrics. Source classification reports F1score (robust to class imbalance): per-class in Table 4, macroaveraged in the ablation  (Table 6)  . Regression tasks report R2 () and σMAD = 1.4826 median(r median(r)) (), robust dispersion estimate (Leung and Bovy 2019), with = ˆy y, or = (ˆz z)/(1 + z) for redshift. Redshift additionally reports the catastrophic-outlier rate, the percentage with > 0.15 (Ilbert et al. 2008), which σMAD by construction ignores (Bolton et al. 2012).

Cross-Survey Generalization We pretrain the three variable-length models (OmniSpectra, Shen et al., Perceiver) on SDSS alone (38009200 Å) and evaluate on DESI and APOGEE with no further pretraining. APOGEE (1510017000 Å) lies entirely outside that range, testing transfer to unseen physical coordinates. OmniSpectra nonetheless transfers with little degradation (Fig. 7a): both wavelength-encoding models stay robust, OmniSpectra with the higher average, whereas Perceivers index-based encoding degrades sharply on redshift. Inference Efficiency Native-pixel patching scales encoder sequence length with the observed spectrum rather than fixed grid. On identical DESI batches (Fig. 7b, batch size 64), OmniSpectra and Shen et al. process shorter sequences and reach the highest throughput, OmniSpectra with far less memory than perpixel and fixed-length baselines. For AstroCLIP (370M) and AION-1 (314M), we count only parameters active on spectral input. Limitations The positional encoding is defined as continuous function of log-wavelength and can therefore be evaluated outside the wavelength union of the training instruments without architectural modification. However, its period range is tuned to approximately 3,60018,000 Å, and performance at substantially different wavelengths has not been evaluated. The learned representations are currently unimodal; extending them to other modalities, for example through CLIP-style alignment, remains future work. Conclusion OmniSpectra tackles pervasive alignment challenge in continuous physical signals: coordinate mismatch across heterogeneous instruments. Built on standard transformer, it replaces integer-indexed embeddings with wavelength-native codes: anchoring position to physical wavelength gives the same feature the same code on any grid, while log-λ turns redshift into an additive shift that cancels in RoPEs relative attention. This reaches state-of-the-art results on classification, redshift, and property regression in fulland lowdata regimes with only 12.2M parameters. The gains come from encoding structure, not pretraining breadth: physicsgrounded inductive biases (log-wavelength translation, hardware resolution gating) offer foundation models more efficient and robust route to alignment.
